blurb_html: Azuki beans simmered soft, then cooked down with sugar into a glossy, chunky paste for daifuku.

chips.html: about 550 g

description: Azuki beans simmered soft, then cooked down with sugar into a glossy, chunky paste for daifuku.

items.amount_html: about 2 L in all

intro_html: Tsubuan is the chunky kind of anko: the beans stay mostly whole in a dark, glossy, just-sweet paste. Azuki don't need soaking. A quick boil and drain takes off the bitter edge, then they simmer until they are soft right through. The sugar goes in only then, because sugar added early keeps the skins hard. Large azuki (dainagon) work the same and take a little longer. Six daifuku take 150–210 g, so one batch fills two or three sets: plain, strawberry daifuku, mame or yomogi.

items: 180 g, in three parts
mise.items_html: 180 g, in three parts
mise.name: Sugar

notes.html:
• After step 3, push the soft beans through a fine sieve with a little of their water, then squeeze the purée dry in a cloth before the sugar goes in.
  • Smooth anko is the classic for daifuku; chunky works just as well.

• 180 g sugar to 200 g beans is the usual, just-sweet amount.
  • Below about 150 g it doesn't keep as long and loosens in the fridge.

• Old beans can take two hours.
  • Keep simmering and keep them covered.
  • Never add the sugar before they crush.

steps.body_html:
• Put the beans in a bowl of cold water and swirl. Lift out anything that floats, plus any split or shrivelled beans and little stones.
  • Drain. No soaking.
steps.title: Rinse

steps.body_html:
• Cover the beans with about 800 ml of cold water and bring it to a boil.
  • Boil 2–3 minutes, until the water turns a cloudy red-brown.
  • Tip into a sieve and rinse the beans under the tap. This water is bitter; it goes down the drain.

how.caption: Boil 2–3 minutes, then tip into the sieve and rinse.

steps.title: Boil once, then drain

steps.body_html:
• Back in the pot with about 1 L of fresh water. Bring to a boil, then turn it down to a gentle simmer with the lid ajar.
  • Keep the beans covered: add a splash of hot water whenever they start to peek out. Beans left above the water stay hard.
  • After 60 minutes, take out a bean and press it between your thumb and ring finger. It's ready when it squashes with no chalky white centre. If not, go on up to 90 minutes.

how.caption: Keep the beans under water: add a splash whenever they peek out.
Done when a bean squashes between thumb and ring finger, no chalky centre.

steps.title: Simmer until a bean crushes

uses_rows.amount_html: about 2 L in all

steps.body_html:
• Pour off water until it sits just below the top of the beans. Keep about a cupful aside.
  • Over medium-low, stir in a third of the sugar. When it has melted, add the next third, then the last, with the salt.
  • The sugar draws water out of the beans, so the pot looks soupy again. That's right.

images.alt: Drain down, sugar in three goes

how.caption: Sugar in three goes over medium-low.

steps.title: Drain down, sugar in three goes

steps.body_html:
• Keep stirring along the bottom with the spatula, scraping the whole base, for 10–15 minutes. It thickens and turns glossy and dark. It also spits, so keep your hand to the side.
  • Drag the spatula across the bottom. Stop when it leaves a trail that closes up slowly.
  • Stop while it's still a little softer than you want. It firms up a lot as it cools. If it's too stiff once cold, stir in a spoonful of the bean water you kept.

images.alt: Stir down until it leaves a trail

how.caption: Keep scraping the whole bottom as it thickens.
Stop when the spatula trail closes up slowly.

steps.title: Stir down until it leaves a trail

steps.body_html:
• Spoon it onto a tray in small mounds so it cools quickly and stays glossy.
  • Press cling film onto the surface so no skin forms.
  • Fridge up to 5 days, or freeze flat in a bag for a month.

how.caption: Small mounds on a tray, cling film pressed onto the surface.

steps.title: Cool fast
